turns.question: We put a pod below an old mine adit. Water is running about pH 3.2 and the conductivity trace looks wrong to me — higher than the grab samples the lab ran. Is the low pH capable of throwing the conductivity off, and if so by how much?
turns.answer:
Yes. When the water is strongly acidic (pH < 4) the usual temperature‑compensation factors used for conductivity can introduce a large error—potentially as much as 50 percent.  

The pod’s configured conductivity‑threshold value is not available here, so I can’t tell you how the reading compares to any internal limit.

A conductivity probe is a very simple device. It is just two conductors with a fixed surface
area at a fixed distance from each other. This distance and surface area is known as the
conductivity cell. The cells distance and surface area is quantified as the conductivity cells
K constant.
How often do you need to
recalibrate a conductivity probe?
Conductivity probes work by measuring the electrical current of the water between two
graphite plates. The plates do not go bad, or change, so recalibration is not necessary. After
the first calibration your conductivity probe is good to go.

reduction is the gain of electrons. The output of the probe is represented in millivolts and
can be positive or negative.
Just like a pH probe measures hydrogen ion activity in a liquid; an ORP probe measures
electron activity in a liquid. The ORP readings represents how strongly electrons are
transferred to or from substances in a liquid. Keeping in mind that the readings do not
indicate the amount of electrons available for transfer.

How often do you need
to recalibrate an ORP probe?
Because every use case is different, there is no set schedule for recalibration.
If you are using your probe in a fish tank, a hydroponic system or any environment that has
generally weak levels of chemical reactions you will only need to recalibrate your probe
once per year for the first 2 years. After that every ~6 months.
If you are using the ORP probe in batch chemical manufacturing, industrial process, or
in a solution that is known to have strong chemical reactions, then calibration should be
done monthly or in extreme cases after each batch.

is proportional to the concentration of hydrogen ions in the liquid being measured.

4.3 Measurement of Specific Conductance of a
Water Sample with Low or High pH
Specific conductance (and electrical conductivity) data
are reported at 25 °C. Most modern specific conductance
meters have the capability to compensate for temperature auto-
matically. Equation 2 is used most commonly to determine the
specific conductance at 25 °C and commercially available field
specific conductance meters typically use either a constant α
(typically 0.019–0.020 per °C) or a nonlinear α (International
Organization for Standardization, 1985). Whereas these com-
monly used temperature-compensation factors work well for
waters having a pH between 4 and 11, they can be the source
of errors as large as 50 percent for low-pH samples.
4.3.1 Measurement of Specific Conductance of
a Water Sample with Low pH (<4)
The specific conductance measurement error for low-pH
(<4) waters can be large if the commonly used temperature-
compensation factors are used. To determine whether an alter-
native temperature-compensation method should be used for
samples with pH <4, the in situ specific conductance should
be compared to the specific conductance of a sample equili-
brated to 25 °C. If the measurements are comparable (within
±5 μS/cm for specific conductance ≤100 μS/cm or ±3 percent
for specific conductance >100 μS/cm), then the temperature
algorithm used is likely sufficient. If a temperature-compen-
sation factor is required for a water sample with pH <4, the
method described by McCleskey (2013) is recommended.
4.3.2 Measurement of Specific Conductance of
a Water Sample with High pH (>11)
No temperature-compensation method is available for
waters with high pH (>11); therefore, the specific conduc-
tance should be checked by making a measurement at ambient
temperature and at 25 °C for waters with pH >11. At high pH,
hydroxide becomes a major ion in the solution and its mobility
is different than that of most other ions. However, the hydrox-
ide-equivalent conductivity is much lower than the hydrogen-
equivalent conductivity and, unlike in low-pH waters, the stan-
dard temperature-compensation approaches may be adequate.
Furthermore, relatively few natural waters have a pH >11, so
this situation is fairly rare.

Accurate and precise measurement of pH in low-specific-
conductance waters (less than 100 μS/cm) is challenging

the electrical circuit and allow for a stable pH reading using
a combination pH electrode, (2) differences in ionic strength
between the sample and buffers are large, and (3) the potential
of the liquid junction is larger than normal. Modern reference
junctions are designed to decrease the effects of low specific
conductance, but may not always produce the desired accuracy

sive, generally are not designed for fieldwork, and only work
well in dilute waters, they do not replace traditional electrodes.

buffers to minimize liquid junction potential errors, but these
buffers are easily contaminated and should be avoided in
field settings.

5.0 	Measurement of pH
Standard procedures for pH measurement are expected
to yield accurate sample pH measurements for waters with
specific conductance between 100 and 60,000 μS/cm, tem-
perature from 0 to 90 °C, and pH from 1.68 to 10. Some of
the procedures will need to be amended to accurately measure
pH at the extremes of these ranges, but standard pH calibra-
tions and combination pH electrodes can be appropriately
used to achieve an accurate pH measurement of environmental
waters whose characteristics fall within these ranges. Studies
of waters whose properties fall outside the ranges described
above (low-ionic-strength waters and [or] waters with pH less
than 1.68 or greater than 10) require further modifications of
pH calibration or measurement procedures.
The pH of sample water should be measured in situ or as
soon as possible after removal of the sample from its environ-
mental source. The pH of a water sample can change substan-
tially within hours or even minutes after sample collection
as a result of temperature change; changes in concentra-
tions of gases (carbon dioxide, hydrogen sulfide, ammonia);
changes in redox conditions; mineral precipitation; metabolic
respiration by microorganisms; and other chemical reac-
tions, physical changes, and biological activity (Hem, 1989).
Field conditions, including rain, wind, cold, heat, dust, direct
sunlight, and direct exposure to vehicle exhaust, can cause
measurement problems. Always protect the instrument system
and the measurement process from the effects of harsh weather
and transportation damage.
In addition to potential changes in the composition of the
sample water, the reliability of pH measurements depends on
the accuracy of the calibration, and temperature measurement.
The physical limitations and characteristics of the electrode,
including response time, liquid junction potentials, and drift,
can affect the accuracy of the pH measurement.

In situ measurements generally are preferred for deter-
mining the specific conductance of surface water, and down-
hole or flow-through cell measurements are preferred for
groundwater. Specific conductance is typically determined on
an unfiltered sample.
• The following precautions should be taken when
measuring specific conductance—
• It is best to measure the specific conductance of the
sample in situ because the specific conductance of
water can change over time as a result of chemi-
cal and physical processes such as precipitation,
adsorption, degassing, and oxidation.
• If a measurement cannot be made in situ and the
water is highly susceptible to substantial gain or
loss of dissolved gases, make the measurement
from a composited or discrete subsample within a
triple-rinsed, gas-impermeable container fitted with
a stopper. Measure the specific conductance as soon
as possible and try to maintain the sample at the
temperature at which it was collected. Gas-bubble
formation on the probe surface or gases flowing over
the surface will result in an inaccurate reading.
• When using multiparameter sondes, avoid
contamination from the pH electrode-filling solu-
tion and calibration buffers. The pH buffers and
filling solutions have high ionic strengths and are a
potential source of contamination. When calibrating
multiparameter sondes, calibrate specific conduc-
tance before pH.
• When measuring the specific conductance of flowing
water, make sure that the conductivity cell has no
cavitation or air bubbles. If the water velocity is too
high to measure the specific conductance accurately,
relocate the probe to an area with lower velocity or
measure the specific conductance of a representative
subsample as soon as possible.
• The stability criterion for recording a specific
conductance measurement in the field is ±5 μS/cm
for measurements ≤100 μS/cm or ±3 percent for
measurements >100 μS/cm. A measurement outside
the criterion is likely the result of air or cavitation
within the conductivity cell, a faulty meter, or poor
mixing of the measured water, causing its composi-

Field measurements, like all measurements of water

7.0 	Reporting
Due to the array of reactions that can change the pH in
environmental samples, the effect of temperature on the opera-
tion of the pH instrument system, and easily changed chemical
and microbiological equilibria within the sample, pH measure-
ments are required to be completed and recorded at the field
site in situ or as soon as possible after removing the sample
from the environmental medium.
Most meters measure with precision in the range of ±0.01
units. Modern meters and multiparameter sondes can some-
times discern environmental patterns within this range. There-
fore, pH should be recorded on field sheets to ±0.01 pH units.
Accuracy of pH measurements is greater at lower values of pH
because hydrogen ion activity is greater. Accuracy of pH mea-
surements is poorer at higher values of pH because the activity
of hydrogen ions is lower.
When recording pH—
• Record the method that was used to make the pH
measurement, as well as the date and serial numbers or
other identifiers for the meter and electrode.
• Record environmental measurements on field sheets
and in NWIS to ±0.01 standard pH units, if the meter
provides this level of precision.
• Rounding for reporting purposes will depend on the
accuracy and precision of the equipment and is typi-
cally to three significant figures. Rounding to ±0.01
units at low and neutral ranges of pH, and to ±0.1 units
for pH values equal to or greater than 10.0, is recom-
mended. The accuracy and precision of the readings for
each meter should be defined further with calibration
checks and quality-control sampling.
• Always record temperature with measurements of pH.
8.0 	Troubleshooting
Consult the instrument manufacturer for recommended
troubleshooting actions for specific single-parameter and
multiparameter pH instrument systems. Many problems
encountered during pH calibration and measurement can be
attributed directly to the condition and responsiveness of the
pH electrode. Depending on use, the typical useful life expec-
tancy of pH electrodes used in environmental field operation
is approximately 12 to 18 months. With time, pH electrodes
need to be evaluated more frequently to determine whether

acceptable response of 95 to 101 percent of the ideal response
slope in NIST-traceable buffers. Replace the pH electrode
when the response falls outside the acceptable range for the
response slope and the deviation cannot be corrected through
cleaning or reconditioning. Also, for any problem encountered,
first check that the instrument batteries are fully charged, and
keep spare fresh batteries on hand.

transferred to or from substances in a liquid. Keeping in mind that the readings do not

2.3 	Standard pH Buffer Solutions
Standard pH buffer solutions (buffers) are ionic solutions
that are used to calibrate the pH meter and electrodes. Buffers
maintain constant pH values (at a single temperature) because
of their ability to resist changes to the specific pH value for
which they are produced. However, the pH of solutions is
affected by temperature, because the calibration slope (which
is related to the Nernst equation) and the isopotential point
change with temperature. Modern pH meters are typically
calibrated with pH buffers having well-known pH-temper-
ature correlations; quality-assured and National Institute of
Standards and Technology- (NIST) traceable pH buffers are
available from USGS One-Stop1. Most pH meters recognize
the e.m.f. range of certain pH buffers (commonly pH 1.68,
4.01, 7.00, and 10.01 buffers) and are able to automatically
compensate for temperature during calibration. Verify that
the buffers you are using are NIST-traceable, that the values
are recognized correctly by the meter, and that the buffers are
compatible with the ATC for your meter. Consult the manu-
facturer’s manual to be sure that the meter will adjust the
expected value of the buffer for the temperature measured. The
user may be responsible for entering the temperature-adjusted
buffer pH value into the meter for calibration from a chart or
the meter may automatically generate a temperature-adjusted
pH value for the buffer.
Measurements of pH are only as accurate as the buffers
used to calibrate the meter and electrodes.
The commonly used pH buffer solutions and their corre-
sponding pH values from 0 to 90 °C are shown in table 6.4–3.
The pH buffers 1.68, 4.01, and 10.01 are primary standards
(pH values determined by using the standard hydrogen-gas
electrode). Their compositions are typically similar for various
manufacturers; therefore, their variations in pH with tem-
perature are well known. The pH-7.00 buffer is a secondary
standard (pH values determined by interpolation to primary
standards) and its composition (and therefore pH dependence
on temperature) may differ with the manufacturer. However,
the pH-7.00 buffer is typically made either from potassium
dihydrogen phosphate plus sodium hydroxide or from potas-
sium dihydrogen phosphate plus sodium hydrogen phosphate;
the pH values of both buffer formulations are comparable to
within 0.02 pH units from 0 to 90 °C.

5.2 	Measurement of pH in Waters with Low

Accurate and precise measurement of pH in low-specific-
conductance waters (less than 100 μS/cm) is challenging
because (1) the water is not sufficiently conductive to complete
the electrical circuit and allow for a stable pH reading using
a combination pH electrode, (2) differences in ionic strength
between the sample and buffers are large, and (3) the potential
of the liquid junction is larger than normal. Modern reference
junctions are designed to decrease the effects of low specific
conductance, but may not always produce the desired accuracy
for measurements of pH. Low-resistance glass pH electrodes
or reference junctions with a fast, continuous leak rate can
be used to make accurate measurements of pH in low-ionic-
strength waters; however, because these electrodes are expen-
sive, generally are not designed for fieldwork, and only work
well in dilute waters, they do not replace traditional electrodes.
Some methods recommend calibrating with low-ionic-strength
buffers to minimize liquid junction potential errors, but these
buffers are easily contaminated and should be avoided in
field settings.

3.0 	Maintenance and Preparation of
pH Instruments
Proper care of pH meters, and particularly of the elec-
trode, is essential for maintaining the accuracy and precision
required for pH measurements and increases the longevity of
the equipment. Maintenance includes adhering to the manufac-
turer's instructions for the use and care of the pH instrument
system, routine electrode cleaning, reconditioning, and storage
requirements. As always, follow the manufacturer’s instruc-
tions for the specific type of electrode in use.
pH-meter and electrode performance is required to be
checked before each water-quality field trip and at each
field site.
3.1 	Electrode Care and Cleaning
USGS field personnel should integrate the following
guidance for the care and cleaning of pH electrodes into their
routine field-measurement procedures.
• Never handle the glass bulb with bare fingers. Oily film
or scratches on the bulb will interfere with the design
characteristics of the glass bulb membrane and affect
pH measurements.
• Inspect the electrode and electrode cable for:
• cut or frayed cable(s)
• broken connectors and mismatched or missing parts
• a visibly scratched or broken glass bulb, cracked
electrode body, and broken or damaged internal
electrodes (reference and measurement electrodes)
• a visibly contaminated reference junction
• low filling solution
• Periodically remove and replace the filling solution
• Gel-filled electrodes do not require filling and typically

5.0 	Measurement of pH
Standard procedures for pH measurement are expected
to yield accurate sample pH measurements for waters with
specific conductance between 100 and 60,000 μS/cm, tem-
perature from 0 to 90 °C, and pH from 1.68 to 10. Some of
the procedures will need to be amended to accurately measure
pH at the extremes of these ranges, but standard pH calibra-
tions and combination pH electrodes can be appropriately
used to achieve an accurate pH measurement of environmental
waters whose characteristics fall within these ranges. Studies
of waters whose properties fall outside the ranges described
above (low-ionic-strength waters and [or] waters with pH less
than 1.68 or greater than 10) require further modifications of
pH calibration or measurement procedures.
The pH of sample water should be measured in situ or as
soon as possible after removal of the sample from its environ-
mental source. The pH of a water sample can change substan-
tially within hours or even minutes after sample collection
as a result of temperature change; changes in concentra-
tions of gases (carbon dioxide, hydrogen sulfide, ammonia);
changes in redox conditions; mineral precipitation; metabolic
respiration by microorganisms; and other chemical reac-
tions, physical changes, and biological activity (Hem, 1989).
Field conditions, including rain, wind, cold, heat, dust, direct
sunlight, and direct exposure to vehicle exhaust, can cause
measurement problems. Always protect the instrument system
and the measurement process from the effects of harsh weather
and transportation damage.
In addition to potential changes in the composition of the
sample water, the reliability of pH measurements depends on
the accuracy of the calibration, and temperature measurement.
The physical limitations and characteristics of the electrode,
including response time, liquid junction potentials, and drift,
can affect the accuracy of the pH measurement.

2.1 	pH Meters
A pH meter is a high-impedance voltmeter that measures
the very small electrical potential (in millivolts [mV]) gener-
ated between a glass bulb pH electrode and a pH reference
electrode (fig. 6.4–2). Combination electrodes are used in most
USGS field studies. They contain both a pH electrode and a
reference electrode in one body and typically connect to the
pH meter by using a multiple pin connector. Modern meters
have a digital display and typically can display pH, electromo-
tive force (e.m.f.) in millivolts, and temperature in degrees
Celsius (°C). The potentiometric measurement is converted
to a pH value either by interpolation or extrapolation with a
standard calibration curve (interpolation is preferred). Meters

multiparameter sonde—

laboratory. Most modern multiparameter sondes auto-matically compensate for temperature differences and
have acceptable accuracy under normal field conditions
for temperatures ranging from 5 to 35 °C and for pH
measurements ranging from 4.0 to 9.5.
• Verify the calibration with measurements of buffers
at ambient field temperatures. Do this regularly to
verify temperature compensation over the range of
temperatures at the site.
2. 	Select the pH-7 buffer and one or two (depending on the
meter) additional buffer solutions that will bracket the
anticipated pH of the sample. Allow the temperature of
the buffers and probes on the sonde to equilibrate.
3. 	Rinse the sonde, calibration cup, and electrode
thoroughly three times with DIW before the calibration
and three times with DIW and buffer solution between
measurement of each buffer solution.
4. 	Rinse the calibration cup, and pH and temperature
sensors, three times with separate aliquots of the first
pH buffer, using the “pour-swirl-discard twice, pour-
sit-discard, pour-sit-measure” method described in
section 4.1.1, step 10.
5. 	Repeat step 4, using additional pH buffers, and lock in
the calibration points. (Depending on site conditions and
study objectives, it might be useful to check the calibra-
tion range of the pH sensor by using an additional buffer;
if appropriate, lock in the third buffer value.)

Slow response times may indicate reduced electrode

For routine cleaning of the pH electrode:
Electrodes must be kept clean and the reference junction
must be flowing freely to obtain accurate pH measurements.
Because a variety of electrodes is available, check the manu-
facturer’s instructions for specific tips and precautions.
• Before and after each use, rinse the electrode body
thoroughly, using only DIW.
• Do not wipe or wick moisture from electrodes with
paper towels or other paper-based wipes, as they can
scratch the glass bulb membrane. Wiping the elec-
trode body with paper also may cause a static charge
(polarization) on the exterior of the pH electrode,
which likewise can adversely affect the pH measure-
ment. Gently shaking electrodes to remove drops of
liquid is recommended. To prepare an electrode for
measurement, rinse it with the solution to be measured
by slowly pouring a small amount of the sample or
buffer to be measured over the electrode. Then place
the electrode into the vessel containing the sample or
buffer, remove the electrode, and dispose of the sample
or buffer. Repeat this process for a total of three times
prior to each pH measurement. To measure the pH
of the sample, add fresh sample or buffer to the same
vessel and then place the electrode directly into the
measurement vessel.
• If using a liquid-filled electrode that has been in a
storage solution for a long time (typically weeks to
months), uncap the fill hole and suspend the electrode
in the air for about 15 minutes. This procedure will
allow the filling solution to flush residual storage
solution through the porous reference junction and
thoroughly wet the junction.
• Soak the electrode (whether gel- or liquid-filled) in
0.1-M HCl for 30 minutes. This procedure removes
many of the solid precipitates that may be fouling the
reference junction. Thoroughly rinse the electrode with
DIW before using or storing.
• If the electrode is contaminated with oil or grease, soak
it in 0.5-percent mild liquid dishwashing detergent
solution for 3 minutes. Thoroughly rinse the electrode
with DIW before using or storing.
• For cleaning bacterial contaminants, soak the electrode
in a dilute (1:10 volume per volume) solution of bleach
(sodium hypochlorite) for 30 minutes. Thoroughly
rinse the electrode with DIW before using or storing.
